response.consequence: The test does not verify that a failed message leaves later offsets committable. A regression that blocks commits after an error would go unnoticed. Whether the test passes depends on where the commit loop's 1s tick falls.
response.explanation: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors must not block offset commits. It then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. In OrderedQueueWorker.run (queue_consumer.py:148-149), the `finally` block calls complete_offset even when the processor raises. The commit loop (queue_consumer.py:273-289) therefore commits offset 102 once it next runs, every ~1s. The test breaks out of its wait loop and sleeps only 0.2s after the queue drains, which is usually before the commit thread fires. The assertion holds only because no commit has happened yet. It does not check the behavior in the docstring, and it would fail if the commit thread ran a little earlier.
response.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implementation and passes only by timing

response.explanation: I traced the per-partition locking in OffsetTracker and the contiguous-offset commit logic. The lock creation in _get_partition_lock is atomic because it uses dict.setdefault. complete_offset runs in a finally block, so it also runs after a failed result_processor. Every submit path adds and then completes the offset, including the decode-None and exception paths. The commit callback in result_consumer.py:249-252 adds +1 to each offset, so the committed value is the next offset to read. One limitation remains. get_committable_offsets stops at any gap in the offset sequence, so a Kafka offset that is never delivered to submit (for example a transaction marker) would stall commits for that partition. Nothing in the snapshot shows that happening for the topics this consumer reads, so I am not reporting it.
response.title: No concrete concurrency or state defect confirmed

response.consequence: The test fails, or at best passes only by timing luck. It also contradicts the implemented behavior, where failed messages are committed and dropped, and no test checks that behavior.
response.explanation: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a `finally` block (queue_consumer.py:148-149), so an offset whose processor raised still counts as complete. In the test, offset 100 raises and offset 101 succeeds. Both end up complete and contiguous, so get_committable_offsets returns 101. The commit loop runs every 1s and calls commit_function, which is commit_offsets (result_consumer.py:249-252). That adds 1 and calls the test's track_commits with {partition: 102}. The test waits about 2.2s at most, which is longer than the 1s commit interval. So committed_offsets contains test_partition when the test reaches `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, and the assertion fails. The docstring says errors don't block commits for other messages, which is the behavior the code has. The assertion says the opposite.

response.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, but the worker completes failed offsets and they get committed

response.consequence: A message that was never processed can have its offset committed. It is then silently dropped instead of redelivered, which breaks the class's "No item is lost" guarantee. This needs a submit failure after queue shutdown, so it is rare.
response.explanation: FixedQueuePool.submit calls offset_tracker.add_offset and then work_queue.put. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) catches any exception from that call and calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. If put raises, for example queue.ShutDown after FixedQueuePool.shutdown has called q.shutdown(), the work item never reached a worker. Its offset is still marked complete. get_committable_offsets then treats it as processed and the commit loop can commit past it. terminate() does not stop the commit thread, so the loop can still commit after the queues are shut down. The shutdown concern in the hypothesis does not cause loss: workers that exit early leave their offsets outstanding, so those offsets are never committed and the messages are redelivered. queue.ShutDown is fine because CLAUDE.md states Python 3.13+. The loss comes from this submit error path.
response.title: Failed queue submission marks the offset completed, so unprocessed messages can be committed

response.consequence: No concrete failing interleaving was found, so no change is needed for this concern.
response.explanation: Every read and write of all_offsets, outstanding and last_committed in add_offset, complete_offset, get_committable_offsets and mark_committed happens inside the partition's lock. The lock is created by _get_partition_lock, which uses dict.setdefault. That call is atomic in CPython, so two threads racing on a new partition end up with the same lock. The list(self.all_offsets.keys()) snapshot avoids a size-change error while iterating. Calling self.all_offsets[partition] while another thread inserts a different key is a single dict operation, and each key's value is only touched under that key's lock. I could not verify the supported Python build from the supplied snapshot, which only covers this one file.
response.title: Per-partition locking is sufficient; no unsynchronized access found

response.consequence: The test is timing-dependent and asserts the opposite of the intended behavior. It can fail intermittently when the commit loop fires. When it passes, it proves nothing about commits after a processing error, and a regression where an error blocks commits would not be caught.
response.explanation: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors must not block offset commits, but it ends with `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a `finally` block (queue_consumer.py:148-149), so the failed message at offset 100 is marked complete along with offset 101. The commit loop (queue_consumer.py:273-289) then calls get_committable_offsets, which returns 101, and commit_offsets turns that into 102. The assertion would only hold if the 1-second commit loop had not run yet. The test waits about 0.2s after the queue drains, so it passes or fails depending on where the commit thread is in its 1s cycle. It does not check the behavior the docstring describes.
response.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting its docstring and the implementation

response.explanation: I read only the supplied diff and source, not the consumer implementation. The added thread-queue-parallel tests wait for the queue pool to drain before asserting. Order is checked per subscription. The offset-gap test expects a commit of 101 and nothing beyond it. The error-handling test expects no commit for the partition once the first message fails. I found no reachable invalid state or lost update in the test code itself. The error-handling test's docstring says failures don't block commits, but its assertion expects no commit. That is a naming mismatch, not a failing case.
response.title: No concrete state-transition defect found in the added tests

response.consequence: On close(), pending queued work is silently dropped. Its offsets stay outstanding and are not committed, so the messages are redelivered after restart. That makes this a delay and duplicate-processing problem rather than data loss. The shutdown also does not drain as designed.
response.explanation: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), which is meant to let queued items drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`. A worker that finishes its current item therefore sees the flag and exits, even though its queue still holds items. Those items are never processed and never completed. Example: a queue holds 100 items when close() runs. The worker finishes the item it is on and returns, leaving the other 99 unprocessed. The docstring says "Gracefully shutdown", and the immediate=False argument shows draining was intended.
response.title: Graceful shutdown does not drain queues because the worker's shutdown flag is set before the queue shutdown

response.explanation: The tests synchronize with locks and events. The processor sets its completion event only after the worker has taken the item off the queue, so the final `qsize()`-based assertion that total_items == 0 holds. The one weak spot is `total_items > 0` right after submit, which can fail if a worker is fast. That is a timing worry, not a defect.
response.title: No concrete concurrency defect found in the new tests

response.consequence: For any partition with an offset gap, commits stop permanently. The consumer re-reads and reprocesses everything since the gap after a restart or rebalance, and the tracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound.
response.explanation: get_committable_offsets walks range(start, max_offset+1) and breaks at the first offset not in all_offsets. After the first commit, start is last_committed+1, so the tracker requires every following offset to be seen. Kafka offsets can have gaps (compacted topics, transaction control markers, filtered or dropped messages not routed through submit). If offset 101 is never submitted, 100 is committed and the loop breaks at 101 on every later pass. The gap is never skipped, so highest_committable stays at last_committed. The same stall happens if a gap exists right after a commit. Nothing clears this state on partition revoke or reassignment, and all_offsets keeps growing because mark_committed never prunes past the gap. I found no code that handles this.

other_findings.consequence: After a restart or rebalance the last processed message of each partition is redelivered and processed again.
other_findings.explanation: The commit loop passes highest_committable, the offset of the last processed message, straight to commit_function. Arroyo and Kafka commit semantics expect the next offset to consume (offset+1). mark_committed also records the same value.
other_findings.title: Commits highest processed offset rather than next offset

response.title: Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits permanently for the partition

response.explanation: The tests synchronize through threading events and a lock. The shared counters and result lists are only updated under the lock. Group-to-queue assignment uses hash(), which is stable within a single process, so the consistency and ordering assertions hold. In test_stats_reporting, the worker removes an item from its queue before processing it, so total_items is 0 once the completion event fires.

response.explanation: I traced the tests against OffsetTracker, FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. The offset-gap, filtered-payload and ordering assertions match the implementation. Filtered messages are added and completed at once, so they do not block commits. A gap at offset 101 holds the commit at 100, and the later commit reaches 103. The only weak spots are timing-dependent assertions, which are out of scope.

response.consequence: After any consumer rebalance, or any strategy close followed by re-creation, every message is dropped without being processed and its offset is committed. This silently loses check-in results, which is data loss in normal operation.
response.explanation: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker. Arroyo creates a new strategy on each partition assignment and closes the old one on each revocation. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate()/join() call queue_pool.shutdown() (queue_consumer.py:335-345), which sets worker.shutdown, calls queue.shutdown() on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance, create_with_partitions builds a new strategy around the same dead pool, so its workers have exited and its queues are shut down. In submit(), FixedQueuePool.submit calls add_offset and then work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The broad except in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (queue_consumer.py:317-325) catches it and marks the offset as added and completed. The commit loop then commits that offset without the message having been processed. The factory's shutdown() also sets queue_pool = None, but strategies keep their own reference.
response.title: Factory-shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by per-assignment strategy close(), then reused after rebalance, silently dropping messages

hypotheses.failure_mode: Offsets are committed as the highest contiguous offset in all_offsets, but contiguity is judged only over offsets seen. Once mark_committed prunes offsets <= committed and last_committed is set, a later-arriving lower offset can be ignored. Also, a gap (e.g. 100,102,103 with 101 not yet received) is bridged: range(start,max+1) breaks at 101 only because 101 is absent from all_offsets, so this works. But the concurrency window between get_committable_offsets and mark_committed lets new offsets be added; and offsets from filtered or skipped Kafka messages that never go through submit are treated as gaps, which can stall commits forever.

Verify gap handling when offsets are legitimately non-contiguous (compacted topics, transaction markers).
